sentences.text: The species of this dinosaur is named Achelousaurus horneri.
It was a large centrosaurine dinosaur, estimated to be about 6 meters long and weigh 3 metric tons.

Adult individuals possessed nasal bosses that were relatively small, thin, and heavily covered with pits, featuring a rough, heavily pitted boss on the snout instead of a horn found in many other ceratopsids.
The neck shield featured two prominent large spikes that pointed backward and curved outward to the sides.
If specimen MOR 591 belongs to Achelousaurus, the genus may have reached adult size faster than Einiosaurus, as it was the same size as a larger Einiosaurus skull but younger.
The genus Achelousaurus was described by Scott D. Sampson in 1994.
The first fossils were collected in Montana in 1987, and all known specimens were recovered from the Two Medicine Formation in Glacier County, Montana.
The informal name Styracosaurus makeli appeared in a book by Stephen Czerkas in 1990 as an invalid nomen nudum.
As a ceratopsian, Achelousaurus was a herbivore with a high metabolic rate.
Oxygen isotope analysis of bones suggests they were homeothermic endotherms.
A 2013 study determined that Achelousaurus was restricted to feeding on vegetation no higher than 1 meter.
Researcher Dodson concluded that monospecific bone beds confirm these dinosaurs lived in herds.
Achelousaurus belongs to the clade Pachyrostra, meaning thick-snouts, within the Ceratopsia.
It lived during the Campanian age as a member of the Centrosaurinae subgroup of ceratopsians.
In 1995, Sampson formally classified Achelousaurus within the Ceratopsidae family, specifically the Centrosaurinae subfamily.
All phylogenetic analyses identify Achelousaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus as sister groups.
Achelousaurus lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 77 to 74.8 million years ago.

These animals lived on a narrow coastal strip on the east coast of Laramidia, bordered by the Western Interior Seaway and the 3 to 4 km high proto-Rocky Mountains, during the phase when the coastal habitat was at its narrowest, experiencing the strongest selection pressures.
The reduced habitat size caused a population bottleneck, which Horner suggested made rapid evolution possible.
Horner proposed that the succession of fossils represented anagenesis, where later forms were simply evolved versions of earlier ones rather than distinct species.
In 1995, Sampson revised the timeline, estimating 860,000 years passed after the Brachyceratops quarry and 640,000 years after the Einiosaurus beds, contradicting Horner's shorter timeframe.

Wilson and colleagues attributed the differences between Einiosaurus and Achelousaurus to heterochrony, or differential development speeds of traits during an individual's lifetime, and in 2020 found Stellasaurus intermediate between Styracosaurus and Einiosaurus in morphology and stratigraphy, supporting its role in an anagenetic lineage.
Scientists debate whether Styracosaurus albertensis or Einiosaurus was the direct ancestor of Achelousaurus.
Some researchers hypothesize that the bumps on Achelousaurus were used in head-butting fights and for display.
